 AMD's AI chip deals with OpenAI, Meta trigger $1 billion charge in Q3 
 Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) recorded a $1.07 billion non-cash charge in the third quarter due to equity warrants offered to OpenAI and Meta Platforms. These warrants are part of agreements for large AI chip commitments. ETElectronicsWorld Desk 
 ETElectronicsWorld 
 Published On Nov 05, 2026 at 07:55 AM IST

 Bookmark 
 Highlights
 AMD recorded a $1.07 billion non-cash charge in Q3 for equity warrants.
 Warrants were granted to OpenAI and Meta Platforms for AI chip commitments.
 Meta's deal involves up to $60 billion in AI chip sales over five years.
 The strategy risks diluting AMD shareholders if warrants fully vest.
 NEW DELHI: Advanced Micro Devices ( AMD ) has recorded a $1.07 billion non-cash charge, or 66 cents a share, in the third quarter ended September 26, Reuters reported on Wednesday. This charge accounts for warrants offered to major artificial intelligence (AI) customers OpenAI and Meta Platforms , as chip shipments under these agreements begin to ramp up. AMD agreed in February to sell up to $60 billion worth of AI chips to Meta over five years. This deal gives Meta warrants that could allow it to buy as much as 10 per cent of the chip firm if certain milestones are met. A similar agreement was made with OpenAI last year, giving the startup an option to buy roughly 10 per cent of the chipmaker. The warrants are part of a growing trend of using equity incentives by chip and AI cloud companies. This strategy aims to secure massive, long-term purchases from a small group of AI customers. It highlights the circular nature of the AI boom, where companies can be customers, suppliers, and investors in one another. The strategy risks diluting AMD shareholders. OpenAI and Meta could own a large stake in the chipmaker for as little as a penny apiece if the warrants fully vest and are exercised. This could substantially increase AMD's share count. The warrants' ultimate value depends on AMD's share price when they are exercised. OpenAI's warrant also includes AMD share-price thresholds, while Meta's does not. Analysts view these deals as a major vote of confidence in AMD's AI chips and software. However, they believe it is unlikely to dent Nvidia's dominance, as the market leader continues to sell every AI chip it can make. AMD also has a chip-purchase arrangement with OpenAI rival Anthropic. That agreement included a commitment by AMD to invest in Anthropic. AMD finance chief Jean Hu stated on Tuesday's analyst call that the warrants would begin diluting AMD shareholders once vesting and exercise conditions are satisfied. These conditions include shipment and other commercial requirements, she said. AMD expects to provide more guidance in 2027 on when those conditions could be met. Other AI chip and infrastructure companies have also struck similar equity-linked deals. Chip startup Cerebras granted OpenAI warrants against a $20 billion commitment. Marvell has issued Alphabet's Google warrants for a potential $12.2 billion stake. Qualcomm gave Amazon warrants in a $60 billion deal for its AI data-center chips.
